title: The Case for Globalizing Fairness: A Mixed Methods Study on Colonialism, AI, and Health in Africa

bias_targets.methodology: Mixed-methods qualitative study (expert surveys, in-depth interviews, and general population surveys across 5 African countries) to assess perceptions on whether the colonial history of a country leads to disparate or biased performance in AI healthcare tools.
Surveys asking experts and general population participants to categorize how likely national income levels and family income levels are to cause an AI tool to perform differently for various groups.
Surveys assessing expert and general population perceptions on whether varying literacy and education levels would lead to disparities in AI tool performance.
Surveys evaluating perceptions on whether a user's country of birth, country of residence, and rural versus urban location would cause an AI tool to exhibit biased behavior.
Surveys asking participants to rate the likelihood that an AI tool would perform differently based on the ethnic or official language spoken by the user.
Surveys measuring perceptions of whether an AI tool would perform differently across different racial groups within the African context.
Surveys assessing perceptions on whether an AI tool would treat users differently or exhibit bias based on their ethnic group.
Surveys measuring expert and general population perceptions on whether skin tone differences would lead to disparate AI model performance.
Surveys assessing participant and expert perceptions on whether gender identity would cause an AI tool to perform differently.
Surveys evaluating perceptions on whether an individual's disability status would lead to disparate performance by an AI healthcare tool.
Surveys assessing perceptions on whether age would cause an AI tool to exhibit biased or disparate performance.
Surveys measuring perceptions on whether an AI tool would treat users differently based on their religious affiliation.
Surveys assessing perceptions on whether a user's sexual orientation would lead to disparate AI tool performance.
Surveys evaluating perceptions on whether pre-existing health conditions, genetics, and physical phenotypes would cause an AI tool to be biased.
